title: Managing an options position
teaches: You get out of an option with the opposite trade; set the target, the stop (on the stock's chart or the option's price) and a re-check date before you buy; take profits in full or in part; treat a roll as a close plus a new trade that costs or pays real money; and deal with short options before expiry, because only a buy-to-close ends assignment risk.

walkthroughs.title: Getting out is a trade
steps: You get out of an option the same way you got in: with a trade, just on the other side.
Bought it, you sell to close. Sold it, you buy to close.
That's how most option positions end. Not with exercise.
Until you close it, that profit is only on paper. It can be a loss tomorrow.

walkthroughs.title: Write the exit before the entry
steps: Before you buy, write down two exits. The target where you take profits, and the stop where you're wrong.
Some traders key a stop off the stock's chart, some off the option's price. Personal preference.
Ours is simpler. We trade shares. On the occasional option buy, the premium you paid is the stop.
Then put a date on the calendar to look at it again. Time decay starts slow and speeds up near expiry.

walkthroughs.title: A roll is two trades
steps: Somebody says just roll it. That means close your option and open a new one at another strike, expiry, or both.
The old one's gain or loss is settled the moment it closes. Rolling doesn't erase it.
Roll a loser and you've locked in the loss. The new option is a fresh trade and needs its own reason.

questions.q: You bought calls last week. The move's done and you want all the way out, holding no shares. What's the order?
questions.why: Sell to close. You got in with a buy, so you get out with a sale of the same contract. FINRA calls it doing the reverse. Most option trades end this way, not with exercise. Exercise is the trap here. It buys you the shares, the opposite of flat. And a put doesn't cancel your call. You'd just own two contracts instead of none.
questions.lesson_line: Bought to open, sell to close. Getting out is just the other side of the trade.

wrong.Buy to close: That's how a seller gets out. You bought this call, so your way out is a sale.
wrong.Exercise the call: Exercising buys you the shares. You wanted out with no shares, so that's backwards.
wrong.Buy a matching put: A put is its own contract and closes nothing. Now you own a call and a put instead of being flat.

questions.simple: Sell to close. You bought to open, so the opposite trade gets you out with no shares.

reasons: stable definition from FINRA and the Options Industry Council, both Tier 1

questions.q: Your call expires Friday and the stock hasn't moved yet. Someone in the chat says just roll it. What would you be doing?
choices: Close it, open a new one
Add contracts at a lower price
questions.answer: Close it, open a new one
questions.why: Close it, open a new one. That's all a roll is. The old option gets sold and a new one gets bought, at another strike, another expiry, or both. The two legs normally go in together. So when you hear roll, think two trades. The new option costs real money, and it has to earn its place like any fresh buy.
questions.lesson_line: A roll is two trades in one ticket: a close and a new open.

wrong.Exercise it before Friday: Exercise turns the option into stock. A roll trades out of one option and into another.
wrong.Add contracts at a lower price: That's averaging down on the same option. A roll replaces the option, it doesn't add to it.
wrong.Move your stop further away: That's widening your stop. A roll swaps the contract itself: the strike, the expiry, or both.

questions.simple: A roll is two trades at once. You close the option you have and open a new one.

reasons: stable definition, Tier 1 glossary plus an agreeing Tier 2 source

questions.q: Planning a call buy with a month left. Next to the target and the stop, a date on the calendar can be an exit too.
questions.why: True. An option runs on a clock, so a date belongs in the plan right next to the price. Pick the day you'll look at it again. If the stock hasn't done its thing by then, time value keeps bleeding while you wait. Some call it a time exit. The date doesn't force a sale. It forces you to ask if the trade is still working.
questions.lesson_line: An option is a bet with a clock on it. Put a re-check date in the plan.
questions.simple: True. A day to look at the trade again belongs in the plan, because time value bleeds while you wait.

reasons: key is only that a date CAN be a trigger; Tier 1 and Tier 2 agree

questions.q: Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: A friend sold a put for the premium. To get out of it, he has to ___ to close.
questions.why: Buy. He opened by selling the put, so he gets out by buying the same put back. Sell again and he's just short two puts. Exercise isn't his call, the put's owner decides that. A roll closes this one but opens another, so he's still short. That's the seller's side, not ours. When you buy an option, your way out is the sale.
questions.lesson_line: Sold to open, buy to close. Bought to open, sell to close.
questions.simple: Buy. A put he sold is closed by buying the same contract back.

reasons: stable definition from FINRA and the Options Industry Council

questions.q: You bought calls and want a stop order working in case you're wrong. How does a stop on an option work?
choices: You pick the trigger, stock or option
Only the option's price can trigger it
Once hit, it has to be a limit order
questions.answer: You pick the trigger, stock or option
questions.why: You pick. The trigger can be the stock's price or the option's price, whichever you'd rather watch. Most exchanges take option stops, but check that your broker does before you count on one. When it fires, it turns into a market order or a limit order, so know which one you set. Our own risk on a bought option is simpler. The premium you paid is the stop, so size it knowing all of it can go.
questions.lesson_line: An option stop can key off the stock or the option. Check that your broker takes it.

wrong.Only the option's price can trigger it: The stock can trigger it too. E*TRADE's contingent order closes an option when the stock hits your price.
wrong.Exchanges won't take option stops: It's the reverse. Most exchanges allow them. Just check that your broker accepts them.
wrong.Once hit, it has to be a limit order: It can be either. Once triggered, an option stop becomes a market order or a limit order.

questions.simple: You choose. The trigger can be the stock's price or the option's price.

reasons: touches the owner's rulebook B25 (options: the premium paid is the stop)
question re-asked 2026-11-12 to remove a both-of-the-above tell

questions.q: Your call expires this week. You want the same strike, just more time. Which roll is that?
questions.why: Rolling out. Out is about time. You close this week's call and open the same strike in a later expiry. tastylive says rolling out always adds time, and you'll hear it called rolling forward too. Up and down are about the strike: up is higher, down is lower. Just know the extra time isn't free. A later expiry carries more time value, so you pay more for it.
questions.lesson_line: Out is time. Up and down are the strike.

wrong.Rolling up: Up moves you to a higher strike. You wanted the same strike with more time.
wrong.Rolling down: Down moves you to a lower strike. Your strike stays put here.
wrong.Rolling up and out: That changes the strike and the expiry. You only wanted more time.

questions.simple: Rolling out, because out means a later expiry, while up and down change the strike.

reasons: stable definition, two Tier 2 publishers agree plus the Tier 1 glossary

questions.q: You're about to buy calls on a breakout. When do you decide where you take profit and where you're out?
questions.why: Before you hit buy. Right now you're calm and nothing's on the line. Once it's open, every tick pulls at you, and not wanting to take the loss starts making the calls. A plan written ahead holds up better. So write it down first: the target, the stop, a date to look again. On an option our stop is simple, the premium you paid. Then do what you wrote.
questions.lesson_line: Write the target and the stop before the order. Then follow them.

wrong.Once it shows a profit: Now you're deciding with money on the screen. That's when emotion makes the call for you.
wrong.When expiry gets close: By then time decay is speeding up against you. The plan comes before the entry, not at the end.
wrong.After it moves against you: That's when loss aversion makes it hardest to act. Set the stop while you're calm.

questions.simple: Before you buy, because a plan made while you're calm is less swayed by emotion.

reasons: fixed before (2026-11-09 checker)

questions.q: Rolling a losing call out to a later month wipes out the loss on the first call.
questions.why: False. A roll sells the first call, and that sale books the loss right there. tastylive is blunt about it: rolling a loser locks in the losing trade. What you hold after is a brand new call, bought at today's price with fresh money. It feels like the same trade. It isn't. Judge the new call the way you'd judge any other buy.
questions.lesson_line: A roll books the loss. It doesn't hide it.
questions.simple: False. The roll sells the first call and books its loss, and the new call is a separate trade.

reasons: Tier 1 glossary plus two agreeing Tier 2 publishers

questions.q: You bought 6 calls at $1.80. A week later they're $3.60, and you sell 3 into the push. How much cash comes back?
questions.why: $1,080. Three contracts at $3.60 is $10.80, and one contract is 100 shares, so that's $1,080. Now look at what all 6 cost you: 6 at $1.80, times 100, is also $1,080. Half the contracts at twice the price, same money. Your cost is back in the account. Worst case the 3 you kept go to zero and you break even, fees aside. That's why I like selling some into strength.
questions.lesson_line: Sell half at a double and your cost is back. The rest rides free.
questions.simple: $1,080, because 3 contracts at $3.60 times 100 is what all 6 cost at $1.80.

deeper.example: Say the stock reverses and the 3 calls you kept go to zero. You took in $1,080 on the 3 you sold, which is what all 6 cost. You end at break-even before fees. Hold all 6 into that same reversal and you lose everything you paid.

reasons: computed key
fixed before (lesson line, 2026-11-09)

wrong.$540: That's the 3 sold at the old $1.80. They're $3.60 now.
wrong.$2,160: That counts all 6 at $3.60. You only sold 3.
wrong.$10.80: That's the per-share number. One contract is 100 shares, so multiply by 100.

questions.story: You bought a call and it's bid $4.00. You set a sell trailing stop $1.50 under the bid. Over the next days the bid runs to $6.20, then rolls over.
questions.q: Where does your trailing stop trigger?
questions.why: $4.70. The trail sits $1.50 under the highest bid. It started at $2.50, under your $4.00, and climbed with every new high. At the $6.20 high it's at $4.70, and it never steps back down. When the bid falls through $4.70, it fires as a market order. So expect a fill near the bid at that moment, not exactly $4.70.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop follows a winner up and never steps back down.

wrong.$2.50: That's where the stop started. It moved up as the bid climbed.
wrong.$4.00: That's the bid when you set it. The stop trails the high, not your start.
wrong.$6.20: That's the high itself. The stop sits the trail amount under it.

questions.simple: $4.70, because the stop trails the $6.20 high by $1.50 and never moves back down.

reasons: computed key

questions.q: A friend buys a call for $3.20. His plan: out at a 50% loss. At what option price does he sell?
questions.why: $1.60. Half of $3.20 is $1.60, so that's his line. E*TRADE says some traders run it this way: out at a double, or out at a 50% loss. It's a real plan, just not ours. For us the premium you paid is the stop. On a $3.20 call, the whole $3.20 is the risk, and you buy knowing that.
questions.lesson_line: Cutting at half is one plan. Ours for options: the premium paid is the stop.
questions.simple: $1.60, because losing half of a $3.20 call leaves it worth $1.60.

reasons: computed key
touches the owner's rulebook B25 (options: the premium paid is the stop); reveal now states the house rule
fixed before (question text, 2026-11-09)

wrong.$4.80: That adds 50% instead of taking it off.
wrong.$6.40: That's double the premium, a profit level. His exit is on the loss side.

questions.story: You own 4 calls from $2.50. They're $4.10 now, with a month left. You think there's more in it, but you don't want the whole gain riding on it.
questions.q: What's the play?
questions.why: Sell 2, let 2 ride. They've gone from $2.50 to $4.10, so selling 2 banks real money and you still have 2 working if it keeps going. That's how I like to handle a winner: some off into strength, the rest stays in. The 2 you keep can still give it all back if it turns, so they need a plan too. Exercising is the mistake here. It throws away the time value left and ties up cash for shares.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some into strength, keep some for the run.

wrong.Hold all 4 for now: That lets the whole gain ride with the full risk of a reversal. It locks in nothing.
wrong.Buy 4 more now: That doubles your contracts at a higher price. It adds risk instead of banking gain.
wrong.Exercise 2, keep 2: Exercise throws away the time value left and needs cash for the shares.

questions.simple: Sell 2 and let 2 ride. Selling part locks in some gain, and the rest stays in for more.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A11 (sell some into strength), consistent with it
fixed before (2026-11-09 checker)

questions.q: Your 50 call has run to $7.00. You sell it and buy the 55 call at $3.50 to stay in the move. Cash back per contract?
questions.why: $350. You take in $7.00 on the 50 call and pay $3.50 for the 55. That's $3.50 a share back, times 100, so $350 a contract. You're still in the move, with some of the profit off the table. Just know the 55 call is a fresh $3.50 bet. For us that premium is the stop, and all of it can go.
questions.lesson_line: Rolling a winner up takes cash off the table and keeps you in the move.
questions.simple: $350 comes back, because you take in $7.00 and pay $3.50, times 100 shares.

reasons: computed key

wrong.$3.50: That's per share. One contract covers 100 shares.
wrong.$1,050: That adds the two prices. You sold one call and bought the other.
wrong.$700: That's only the sale of the 50 call. You spent $350 of it on the 55.

questions.q: A friend buys back his short call at noon. That call can't be assigned to him tonight.
questions.why: True. Once he buys it back, the short call is gone, and only an open short can be assigned. OCC handles closing buys before exercises, and assignment goes by his net position after the close. So a call closed at noon is off the table. One check: make sure with the broker it wasn't assigned already. That's the seller's side, not ours. It's also why sellers say: when in doubt, close them out.
questions.lesson_line: When in doubt, close them out. A short option you've bought back can't be assigned.
questions.simple: True. A short call he bought back is no longer open, and only open shorts get assigned.

reasons: fixed before (2026-11-09 checker added f90)

questions.story: A friend sold a call spread. The stock ripped through his short strike, so he rolls the spread up to higher strikes and out a month.
questions.q: What did the roll do to his assignment risk?
choices: Cut it, but didn't end it
Ended it, the strike is higher now
Raised it, since it runs longer
Moved it onto his long call
questions.answer: Cut it, but didn't end it
questions.why: Cut it, but didn't end it. The new short call sits at a higher strike with more time, so assignment is less likely. But he's still short a call, and an open short can be assigned. The Options Industry Council says it straight: rolling reduces the risk, only buying back removes it. That's the seller's side, not ours. When you buy an option, nobody can assign you. You decide whether to exercise.
questions.lesson_line: A roll moves a short option's risk. Only a buy-to-close ends it.

wrong.Ended it, the strike is higher now: He's still short a call. As long as a short option stays open, it can be assigned.
wrong.Raised it, since it runs longer: Assignment risk grows deeper in the money and nearer expiry. A higher strike and more time cut it.
wrong.Moved it onto his long call: A long option can't be assigned. Its holder decides whether to exercise.

questions.simple: Cut but not ended. He's still short a call after the roll, and an open short can be assigned.

reasons: Tier 1 source states this exact case (OIC April 2026 FAQ)

questions.q: Your call expiring Friday is bid $0.90 and the stock hasn't moved. The same strike two months out costs $3.10. Cost to roll?
questions.why: $220. You sell the old call at the $0.90 bid and pay $3.10 for the new one. That's $2.20 a share, times 100, so $220 out of your pocket. More time means more time value, which is why the later month costs more. And that new $3.10 premium is your new stop. Here's my test. If you wouldn't buy that call fresh today, don't roll into it.
questions.lesson_line: Rolling a long option out isn't free. Every month you add is paid for, and it can be lost.
questions.simple: $220, because you get $0.90 for the old call and pay $3.10 for the new one, times 100.

deeper.counter: A roll out can feel like keeping the same trade alive. It isn't. You booked $0.90 on the old call and paid $3.10 for a new one. If the stock still doesn't move, time decay works on the new call too. It starts slowly, then speeds up near expiry, and the premium you paid is what you can lose.

reasons: computed key

wrong.$400: That adds the two prices. You sell one call and buy the other.
wrong.$310: That's only the new call. It forgets the $0.90 you get back.
wrong.$2.20: That's per share. One contract covers 100 shares.

questions.q: A fund sold a put spread for $1.20. It costs $0.25 to close now. Hold to expiry instead: the most extra it can make per spread?
questions.why: $25. On a credit spread, the $1.20 credit is the most there is to make. Closing costs $0.25, so holding can add at most that $0.25 a share. Times 100, that's $25. For that $25 the fund keeps the spread's full risk until expiry. tastylive makes the same point about a short option near max profit. That's the seller's side, not ours. But you can use the idea: when nearly all the money's made, holding pays little.
questions.lesson_line: Near max profit, a short spread pays little to hold and keeps all its risk.
questions.simple: $25 is the most extra, because only the $0.25 it costs to close is left to earn, times 100.

reasons: computed key

wrong.$120: That's the whole credit. Most of it is already made.
wrong.$95: That's what closing now locks in, not what's left to make.
wrong.$145: That adds the $0.25 closing cost to the $1.20 credit.

questions.story: It's expiry day. A friend's short put is in the money, and he'd rather roll it out a month than take the shares.
questions.q: How should he work the roll?
choices: Well before the close, as one order
Close now, sell the new put later
Let it expire, then sell a new put
questions.answer: Well before the close, as one order
questions.why: Well before the close, as one order. Both legs go in together, so the stock can't move on him in between. Schwab says liquidity can dry up near the close on expiry day, and spreads can widen. So sooner is better. Letting it expire is the worst choice here. In the money at expiry, it's most likely exercised, and he gets the shares he wanted to avoid. That's the seller's side, not ours. The same timing holds when you sell a long option on expiry day.
questions.lesson_line: On expiry day, get your business done early, in one order. Don't leave it to the bell.

wrong.Close now, sell the new put later: That splits the roll into two trades, and the stock can move in between.
wrong.Let it expire, then sell a new put: In the money, it's most likely exercised, and he gets the shares he wanted to avoid.
wrong.Wait for the final minutes: That's when liquidity can dry up and spreads widen. Schwab says sooner may be better.

questions.simple: Roll early in one order, because late on expiry day buyers thin out and spreads widen.

deeper.trap: The trap is waiting to see if the put finishes out of the money. In the final minutes, liquidity can dry up and spreads may widen. An in-the-money option is generally exercised at expiry. So the short put is likely assigned, and he gets the shares he meant to avoid.

reasons: touches the owner's rulebook E57 (market orders: the limit was dropped from the key) and A6 (options only as a defined-risk alternative)
fixed before (2026-11-09 checker)

questions.story: Your call is down 60% with a week left. The stock broke the level your plan was built on. A friend says roll it out three months.
questions.q: What would that roll really be?
choices: Taking the loss, then a new bet
A patient way to wait out the dip
A free extension of the call
Just more time on the same trade
questions.answer: Taking the loss, then a new bet
questions.why: Taking the loss, then a new bet. The roll sells the old call, so that 60% loss is booked right there. tastylive says rolling a loser locks in the losing trade and opens a new one. The three-month call costs more too, because more time means more time value. And here's the real problem: the level your plan stood on broke. The reason for the trade is gone. I close it. If a new setup shows up later, I buy that on its own.
questions.lesson_line: If the setup broke, I close it. Rolling a broken idea is just buying it again.

wrong.A free extension of the call: The later call has more time value, so it costs more. You pay for those extra months.
wrong.Just more time on the same trade: The old call is closed and its loss booked. The new call is a separate trade at today's price.
wrong.A patient way to wait out the dip: The level your plan stood on broke. tastylive calls a rolled loser a new low probability trade.

questions.simple: Taking the loss and a new bet, because the roll closes the old call before it opens a new one.

deeper.trap: Rolling out feels like patience. But the old call is closed at a loss, and the money for the new call is fresh risk. The new call needs a reason of its own. Your plan's reason, the level the stock broke, is gone. Without a new reason, closing beats rolling.

reasons: fixed before (distractor replaced 2026-11-09)

questions.q: If an option trades on an exchange, you can always find a buyer when you want out.
questions.why: False. Listed doesn't mean liquid. There's no promise a market exists for every option at all times. A wide spread, or no bid at all, is how you get stuck in one. So look at the bid and the spread before you buy, not when you need out. An exit you can't fill isn't an exit.
questions.lesson_line: Check the bid and the spread before you buy. An exit you can't fill isn't an exit.
questions.simple: False. There's no promise of a market to sell in for every option at all times.

deeper.trap: An option can look great on paper and still be hard to sell. FINRA says profits aren't guaranteed until a closing trade is done. The disclosure document says a market may not exist for every option at all times. So the time to check the bid and the spread is before you buy, not when you need out.

reasons: fixed before (why split, 2026-11-09)

questions.story: tastylive, the options network, sells options for a credit. It says it usually rolls a short option 7 to 21 days before expiry.
questions.q: What's it trying to get away from?
questions.why: Gamma and assignment risk. tastylive names both. Near expiry, gamma jumps on an at-the-money option, so a small stock move swings the price hard. And the closer expiry gets, the likelier an open short gets assigned. Faster decay actually helps a seller, so that's not the threat. That's the seller's side, not ours. What you take from it: an option near the money swings hardest in its last weeks.
questions.lesson_line: Near expiry, an option near the money can swing fast. Decide early whether to close or roll.

wrong.A drop in implied volatility: Falling volatility tends to lower option prices. That helps a seller, so it isn't what they're running from.
wrong.Time decay slowing down: Decay speeds up near expiry, and that helps a seller. The danger is how fast the price can swing.
wrong.The stock sitting still: Short options gain when the stock sits still. Their risk is a sharp, sudden move.

questions.simple: Gamma and assignment risk, because near expiry a short option near the money swings fast and is likelier to be assigned.

deeper.trap: Fast decay in the last weeks looks like free money for a seller. The same weeks bring a sharp rise in gamma for at-the-money options, so a small stock move can swing the option hard. tastylive's 7 to 21 days is its own practice, not a rule. The point is to decide early whether to close or roll.

reasons: story carries tastylive's own 7 to 21 day practice, which can change
fixed before (2026-11-09 checker)

questions.q: Holding a big winning call to expiry is risk-free, since you can't lose more than the premium.
questions.why: False. The premium caps what you can lose of your own money. It doesn't cap what you can give back. FINRA says profits aren't guaranteed until you close the trade. So a call that's up big is still a paper gain, and a reversal can take all of it. Holding to expiry risks the gain, not just the cost. That's why I sell some into strength instead of hoping.
questions.lesson_line: The premium caps the loss. Nothing caps how much open profit you can give back.
questions.simple: False. The premium caps your loss on what you paid, not the open profit you can give back.

deeper.trap: Traders mix up two caps. The premium caps what you can lose of your own money. Nothing caps how much open profit you can hand back. A call that's well up is a paper gain until you sell it, and a reversal can take all of it.

reasons: Tier 1 sources (OIC, FINRA) agree

questions.story: You own calls with a sell stop on the option at $2.00. Bad news hits, and the bid drops straight to $1.40.
questions.q: Your stop turns into a market order. Where does it most likely fill?
questions.why: Near $1.40, at the bid. A triggered stop is a market sell, and a market sell takes the best bid there is. The $2.00 was only the trigger, never a promised price. Schwab warns the fill can come in well under the stop. A stop-limit would hold out for $2.00, but then you might not get out at all while it keeps falling. A stop picks when you get out, not the price. On an option you bought, the premium paid is still your worst case.
questions.lesson_line: A stop picks when you get out, not the price. In a fast market, expect the bid.

wrong.At $2.00, your stop price: The stop is a trigger, not a promised price. Once it fires, it takes the bid.
wrong.Not until $2.00 trades again: That's how a stop-limit behaves. It can leave you holding while the price keeps falling.
wrong.At the ask, just above $1.40: A market sell fills at the best bid, not the ask. The Options Industry Council says so directly.

questions.simple: Near $1.40, because a triggered stop is a market sell, and that sells at the best bid there is.

deeper.trap: Many traders think a stop guarantees its price. It doesn't. Here the bid dropped straight from above $2.00 to $1.40, so the market order took about $1.40. A stop-limit at $2.00 would not fill until $2.00 traded again, which may not happen while the price keeps falling.

reasons: touches the owner's rulebook B25 (premium paid is the stop) and D41 (real stop orders)

questions.story: Your calls are up 150% with three weeks left. The stock just hit the target your plan set for its whole move.
questions.q: What do you do with them now?
questions.why: Take the profit, close it. The stock hit the target your plan set for the whole move. You picked that target when you were calm, so trust it. The reason you bought is used up. Holding for more is a new plan made in the rush of a win. And with three weeks left, time decay is speeding up against you. I'd rather book 150% than hand it back.
questions.lesson_line: When the stock hits the target you set, take it. You made that call when you were calm.

wrong.Hold for more, it's working: That's a new plan made on the fly. Letting it ride means taking the risk of a reversal.
wrong.Roll up and add contracts: Adding contracts adds risk right when your plan says the move is done.
wrong.Exercise and keep the shares: Exercise throws away the time value left, and it needs cash for the shares.

questions.simple: Take the profit, because the stock already made the move your plan expected, so the reason to hold is gone.

deeper.trap: A 150% gain makes it feel like the trade is still working, so why stop? But the reason you bought is used up: the stock hit the target for its whole move. Anything more is a new bet with your profit at stake. It is made in the rush of a win, not with the calm plan.

reasons: touches the owner's rulebook A11 and E51 (trims and a trail, for shares)
fixed before (question text, 2026-11-09)

questions.story: A friend sold a put for $0.80. He follows tastylive's rule: close a losing short option at a net loss of twice the credit.
questions.q: At what price does he buy the put back?
questions.why: $2.40. On a short option, the loss is what you pay to buy it back minus the credit. Twice the $0.80 credit is $1.60 of loss. So he buys back at $0.80 plus $1.60, which is $2.40, three times the credit. tastylive's own example works the same: collect $1.00, close at $3.00, a $2.00 loss. That's tastylive's rule and the seller's side, not ours. Still, it's how you read a friend's short: loss is buy-back minus credit.
questions.lesson_line: On a short option, the loss is the buy-back price minus the credit taken in.

wrong.$1.60: That's twice the credit as a price. Buying back there loses only one times the credit.
wrong.$0.80: That's where he sold it. Buying back there is break-even, not a stop.
wrong.$0.40: That cuts the credit in half instead of tripling it.

questions.simple: $2.40, because a loss of twice the $0.80 credit means paying back the credit plus twice it.

deeper.trap: The common slip is to buy back at twice the credit, $1.60. That price loses only one times the credit. The rule counts the net loss, not the option's price. It's tastylive's practice, and tastylive says only that it found this can be optimal. We don't use it.

reasons: computed key on tastylive's own rule, a practice that can change
touches the owner's rulebook A6 and B25 (options only as a defined-risk alternative)

questions.q: You buy calls on a breakout, one of the rare times you use options instead of shares. Where's your stop?
choices: A level on the stock's chart
questions.why: The premium you paid. That's our rule for options, with no further rules on top: the premium paid is the stop. A buyer can't lose more than the premium, so that number is the whole risk. You know your worst case the second you click buy. So size it knowing the whole premium can go.
questions.lesson_line: For us, an option's stop is the premium paid. A buyer can't lose more than that.

wrong.A level on the stock's chart: The Options Industry Council leaves the trigger to you. We've picked ours: the premium paid is the stop.
wrong.Half the premium you paid: Some traders cut at a 50% loss, E*TRADE says. That's their plan. Ours is the premium paid.
wrong.No stop needed on options: There's always a stop. On an option you buy, it's the premium you paid.

questions.simple: The premium you paid. On an option you buy, that's our stop and your whole risk.

reasons: house rule B25, quoted from the owner's rulebook (sizing_rule.md section 9)

questions.q: We trade shares. Options are a defined-risk alternative we use only now and then.
questions.why: True. Shares are what we trade. An option is the occasional alternative. The draw is defined risk: the premium paid is the stop, and that's all it can cost. We don't stack more rules on top. So most of what you trade with us is shares, sized off the stop on the chart.
questions.lesson_line: We trade shares. Options are an occasional, defined-risk alternative.
questions.simple: True. We trade shares and use options only now and then, with the risk set by the premium.

reasons: house rules A6 and B25, quoted from the owner's rulebook (sizing_rule.md section 9)

conflicts: The '21-day rule' in the unit plan: the version usually repeated ('manage short options at 21 days to expiry') is credited to tastytrade's research, but the tastylive page that could be fetched (s22) says it rolls '7-21 days prior to expiration'. No day count is keyed as a rule: q21 gives tastylive's own 7-21 practice as a given and keys only the reason, which OIC (Tier 1) states on its own (gamma rises sharply as time is removed, f37; assignment risk grows as expiration approaches, f28; decay accelerates in the last three weeks, f35).

Profit and loss percentages and multiples: E*TRADE's example exits at double or at a 50% loss (f65); tastylive closes short-premium winners at 50% of max profit (s21, not quoted as a fact) and says closing a loser at a net loss of 2x the credit 'can be optimal' (f88). Per the unit plan, no percentage or multiple is keyed as UCT's rule or as best practice. q11 states the member's own plan ('out if it loses half its value') and names E*TRADE's example only in the reveal; q25 gives tastylive's 2x rule in the story as tastylive's and keys only the arithmetic (a loss of twice the credit means buying back at three times it), which tastylive's own $1.00 / $3.00 example states (f89); q17 computes from given prices and cites tastylive only for the risk/reward point (f70). tastylive's 'optimal' claim rests on its own back-tests and is not repeated.

OIC's long call page says some buyers set price targets or re-evaluation dates while 'others play it by ear' (f02). q07 ('decide the exit before you buy') is keyed on Fidelity (f50) and E*TRADE (f60, f61), two Tier 2 publishers that agree; OIC is not cited as saying a plan is required, and q03 keys only that a date CAN be an exit trigger (OIC f02 plus Fidelity's time exit, f77).

Trailing stops on options: E*TRADE's example trails the option's bid by a fixed dollar amount (f78); Schwab's trailing-stop page (f80, f81) is written for stocks. Both say a sell trailing stop only moves up and becomes a market order when triggered. q10 keys only that mechanic (calc: high minus trail); whether a given broker trails the bid, the last trade or the mark is not keyed.

What triggers a stop order on an option (a trade, or the bid or offer) has differed by exchange and over time in Cboe's rule filings. The file never keys the trigger mechanics; q23 says only that a stop that has turned into a market sell order fills at the best bid (OIC, f21) and can fill well under the stop (Schwab, f58).

Investopedia's roll-up example (s20) reads 'either selling the June call option or by simultaneously buying' a September call; the roll it then describes is a sell and a buy together. q13's key rests on OIC's FAQ (f18, Tier 1: sell the options, then buy a more distant strike for a credit); the Investopedia line (f67) is cited only for 'protecting part of the profits'.

Schwab's 'When Should I Roll My Options Trades?' (November 25, 2025) is a video with no page text and is not cited. Fidelity's 'Rolling covered calls' (written by The Options Institute at Cboe) was read but is about covered calls (F6.13's ground) and is not cited.

Expiry-day times (Schwab's 3 p.m. CT trading cut-off, OCC's exercise thresholds and deadlines) change with products and rules and belong to F6.16. f53 is quoted for its point that liquidity thins near the close; no question asks for a time.
Every dollar figure ignores commissions and fees, as OIC's own examples do ('less commission, of course').
